sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen15353" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Song.8" sID="Song.8"/> <div eID="gen15353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15354" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15355" type="x-p"/> The affections between Christ and his spouse are as strong and lively here, in this closing chapter of the song, as ever, and rather more so. I. The spouse continues her importunity for a more intimate communion and fellowship with him, <reference osisRef="Song.8.1-Song.8.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to interrupt her communion with her beloved (<reference osisRef="Song.8.4">ver. 4</reference>); and they, thereupon, admire her dependence on him, <reference osisRef="Song.8.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. She begs of her beloved, whom she raises up by her prayers (<reference osisRef="Song.8.5">ver. 5</reference>), that he would by his grace confirm that blessed union with him to which she was admitted, <reference osisRef="Song.8.6-Song.8.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. She makes intercession for others also, that care might be taken of them (<reference osisRef="Song.8.8-Song.8.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), and pleases herself with the thoughts of her own interest in Christ and his affection to her, <reference osisRef="Song.8.10">ver. 10</reference>. V. She owns herself his tenant for a vineyard she held of him at Baal-hamon, <reference osisRef="Song.8.11-Song.8.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. VI. The song concludes with an interchanging of parting requests. Christ charges his spouse that she should often let him hear from her (<reference osisRef="Song.8.13">ver. 13</reference>), and she begs of him that he would hasten his return to her, <reference osisRef="Song.8.14">ver. 14</reference>).

The spouse wishes for a constant intimacy and freedom with the Lord Jesus. She was already betrothed to him, but, the nuptials being yet not solemnized and published (the bride, the Lamb's wife, will not be completely ready till his second coming), she was obliged to be shy and to keep at some distance; she therefore wishes she may be taken for his sister, he having called her so (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1">ch. v. 1</reference>), and that she might have the same chaste and innocent familiarity with him that a sister has with a brother, an own brother, that <hi type="italic">sucked the breasts</hi> of the same <hi type="italic">mother</hi> with her, who would therefore be exceedingly tender of her, as Joseph was of his brother Benjamin. Some make this to be the prayer of the Old-Testament saints for the hastening of Christ's incarnation, that the church might be the better acquainted with him, when, <hi type="italic">forasmuch as the children are partakers of flesh and blood,</hi> he should also himself likewise take part of the same, and not be ashamed to call them brethren. It is rather the wish of all believers for a more intimate communion with him, that they might <hi type="italic">receive the Spirit of sanctification,</hi> and so Christ must be as their brother, that is, that they might be as his brethren, which <hi type="italic">then</hi> they are when by grace they are made partakers of a divine nature, and <hi type="italic">he that sanctifies, and those that are sanctified, are both of one,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.11">Heb. ii. 11</reference>, &c. It becomes brethren and sisters, the children of the same parents, that have been nursed at the same breast, to be very loving to and tender of one another; such a love the spouse desires might be between her and her beloved, that she might call him brother. 2. She promises herself then the satisfaction of making a more open profession of her relation to him than at present she could make: "<hi type="italic">When I should find thee without,</hi> any where, even before company, <hi type="italic">I would kiss thee,</hi> as a sister does her own brother, especially her little brother that is now <hi type="italic">sucking the breasts of her mother</hi>" (for so some understand it); "I would use all the decent freedom with thee that could be, and <hi type="italic">should not be despised</hi> for it, as doing any thing unbecoming the modesty of my sex." The church, since Christ's incarnation, can better own him than she could before, when she would have been laughed at for being so much in love with one that was not yet born. Christ has become as our brother; wherever we find him, therefore, let us be ready to own our relation to him and affection for him, and not fear being despised for it, nor regard that any more than David did when he danced before the ark. <hi type="italic">If this be to be vile, I will be yet more vile.</hi> Nay, let us hope that we shall not be despised so much as some imagine. <hi type="italic">Of the maid-servants of whom thou hast spoken I shall be had in honour.</hi> Wherever we find the image of Christ, though it be without, among those that do not follow him with us, we must love it, and testify that love, and we <hi type="italic">shall not be despised</hi> for it, but catholic charity will gain us respect. 3. She promises to improve the opportunity she should then have for cultivating an acquaintance with him (<reference osisRef="Song.8.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I would lead thee,</hi> as my brother, by the arm, and hang upon thee; I would show thee all the house of my precious things, would bring <hi type="italic">thee into my mother's house,</hi> into the church, into the solemn assemblies (<reference osisRef="Song.3.4">ch. iii. 4</reference>), into my closet" (for there the saints have most familiar communion with Christ), "and <hi type="italic">there thou wouldst instruct me</hi>" (so some read it), as brethren inform their sisters of what they desire to be instructed in. Those that know Christ shall be taught of him; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> we should desire communion with Christ that we may receive instruction from him. He has come that he might give us an understanding. Or, "My mother would instruct me when I have thee with me." It is the presence of Christ in and with his church that makes the word and ordinances instructive to her children, who shall all be taught of God. 4. She promises him to bid him welcome to the best she had; she would <hi type="italic">cause him to drink of her spiced wine and the juice of her pomegranate,</hi> and bid him welcome to it, wishing it better for his sake. The exercise of grace and the performance of duty are spiced wine to the Lord Jesus, very acceptable to him, as expressive of a grateful sense of his favours. Those that are pleased with Christ must study to be pleasing to him; and they will not find him hard to be pleased. He reckons hearty welcome his best entertainment; and, if he have that, he will bring his entertainment along with him. 5. She doubts not but to experience his tender care of her and affection to her (<reference osisRef="Song.8.3">v. 3</reference>), that she should be supported by his power and kept from fainting in the hardest services and sufferings <hi type="italic">(His left hand shall be under my head</hi>) and that she should be comforted with his love—<hi type="italic">His right hand should embrace me.</hi> Thus Christ laid his right hand upon John when he was ready to die away, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Rev. i. 17</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Dan.10.10">Dan. x. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.18">18</reference>. It may be read as it is <reference osisRef="Song.2.6">ch. ii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">His left hand is under my head</hi> (for the words are the same in the original) and so it expresses an immediate answer to her prayer; she was answered with <hi type="italic">strength in her soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Ps. cxxxviii. 3</reference>. While we are following hard after Christ his <hi type="italic">right hand sustains us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Ps. lxiii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Underneath are the everlasting arms.</hi> 6. She charges those about her to take heed of doing any thing to interrupt the pleasing communion she now had with her beloved (<reference osisRef="Song.8.4">v. 4</reference>), as she had done before, when he thus strengthened and comforted her with his presence (<reference osisRef="Song.2.7">ch. ii. 7</reference>): Let me <hi type="italic">charge you, O you daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> and reason with you, <hi type="italic">Why should you stir up, and why should you awake, my love, until he will?</hi> The church, our common mother, charges all her children that they never do any thing to provoke Christ to withdraw, which we are very prone to do. Why should you put such an affront upon him? Why should you be such enemies to yourselves? We should thus reason with ourselves when we are tempted to do that which will grieve the Spirit. "What! Am I weary of Christ's presence, that I affront him and provoke him to depart from me? Why should I do that which he will take so unkindly and which I shall certainly repent of?"

She was already betrothed to him, but, the nuptials being yet not solemnized and published (the bride, the Lamb's wife, will not be completely ready till his second coming), she was obliged to be shy and to keep at some distance; she therefore wishes she may be taken for his sister, he having called her so ( ch. v. 1 ), and that she might have the same chaste and innocent familiarity with him that a sister has with a brother, an own brother, that sucked the breasts of the same mother with her, who would therefore be exceedingly tender of her, as Joseph was of his brother Benjamin. Those that know Christ shall be taught of him; and therefore we should desire communion with Christ that we may receive instruction from him. He has come that he might give us an understanding. Or, "My mother would instruct me when I have thee with me." It is the presence of Christ in and with his church that makes the word and ordinances instructive to her children, who shall all be taught of God. 4. She promises him to bid him welcome to the best she had; she would cause him to drink of her spiced wine and the juice of her pomegranate, and bid him welcome to it, wishing it better for his sake. It may be read as it is ch. ii. 6 , His left hand is under my head (for the words are the same in the original) and so it expresses an immediate answer to her prayer; she was answered with strength in her soul, Ps. cxxxviii. 3 . While we are following hard after Christ his right hand sustains us, Ps. lxiii. 8 . Underneath are the everlasting arms. 6. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen15357" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Church's Dependence on Christ; The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15358" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? I raised thee up under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth <hi type="italic">that</hi> bare thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love <hi type="italic">is</hi> strong as death; jealousy <hi type="italic">is</hi> cruel as the grave: the coals thereof <hi type="italic">are</hi> coals of fire, <hi type="italic">which hath a</hi> most vehement flame. 7 Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if <hi type="italic">a</hi> man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned. <div eID="gen15358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15359" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The spouse is much admired by those about her. It comes in in a parenthesis, but in it gospel-grace lies as plain, and as much above ground, as any where in this mystical song: <hi type="italic">Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?</hi> Some make these the words of the bridegroom, expressing himself well pleased with her reliance on him and resignation of herself to his guidance. They are rather the words of the daughters of Jerusalem, to whom she spoke (<reference osisRef="Song.8.4">v. 4</reference>); they see her, and bless her. The angels in heaven, and all her friends on earth, are the joyful spectators of her bliss. The Jewish church came up from the wilderness supported by the divine power and favour, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.10-Deut.32.11">Deut. xxxii. 10, 11</reference>. The Christian church was raised up from a low and desolate condition by the grace of Christ relied on, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.27">Gal. iv. 27</reference>. Particular believers are amiable, nay, admirable, and divine grace is to be admired in them, when by the power of that grace they are brought <hi type="italic">up from the wilderness, leaning</hi> with a holy confidence and complacency <hi type="italic">upon</hi> Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">their beloved.</hi> This bespeaks the beauty of a soul, and the wonders of divine grace, 1. In the conversion of sinners. A sinful state is a <hi type="italic">wilderness,</hi> remote from communion with God, barren and dry, and in which there is no true comfort; it is a wandering wanting state. Out of this wilderness we are concerned to <hi type="italic">come up,</hi> by true repentance, in the strength of the grace of Christ, supported by our beloved and carried in his arms. 2. In the consolation of saints. A soul convinced of sin, and truly humbled for it, is in a <hi type="italic">wilderness,</hi> quite at a loss; and there is no coming out of this <hi type="italic">wilderness</hi> but <hi type="italic">leaning</hi> on Christ as our beloved, by faith, and not <hi type="italic">leaning to our own understanding,</hi> nor trusting to any righteousness or strength of our own as sufficient for us, but going forth, and going on, in the strength of the Lord God, and making mention of his righteousness, even his only, who is <hi type="italic">the Lord our righteousness.</hi> 3. In the salvation of those that belong to Christ. We must go up from the wilderness of this world having our conversation in heaven; and, at death, we must remove thither, <hi type="italic">leaning</hi> upon Christ, must live and die by faith in him. <hi type="italic">To me to live is Christ,</hi> and it is he that is gain in death. <div eID="gen15359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15360" type="x-p"/> II. She addresses herself to her beloved. <div eID="gen15360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15361" type="x-p"/> 1. She puts him in mind of the former experience which she and others had had of comfort and success in applying to him. (1.) For her own part: "<hi type="italic">I raised thee up under the apple tree,</hi> that is, I have many a time wrestled with thee by prayer and have prevailed. When I was alone in the acts of devotion, retired in the orchard, under <hi type="italic">the apple-tree</hi>" (which Christ himself was compared to, <reference osisRef="Song.2.3">ch. ii. 3</reference>), as <hi type="italic">Nathanael under the fig-tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.48">John i. 48</reference>), "meditating and praying, then <hi type="italic">I raised thee up,</hi> to help me and comfort me," as the disciples raised him up in the storm, saying, <hi type="italic">Master, carest thou not that we perish?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.38">Mark iv. 38</reference>), and the church (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Ps. xliv. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">Awake, why sleepest thou?</hi> Note, The experience we have had of Christ's readiness to yield to the importunities of our faith and prayer should encourage us to continue instant in our addresses to him, to strive more earnestly, and not to faint. <hi type="italic">I sought the Lord, and he heard me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.4">Ps. xxxiv. 4</reference>. (2.) Others also had like experience of comfort in Christ, as it follows there (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.5">Ps. xxxiv. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">They looked unto him,</hi> as well as I, <hi type="italic">and were lightened.</hi> There <hi type="italic">thy mother brought thee forth,</hi> the universal church, or believing souls, in whom Christ was formed, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.15">Gal. iv. 15</reference>. They were in pain for the comfort of an interest in thee, and <hi type="italic">travailed in pain</hi> with <hi type="italic">great sorrow</hi> (so the word here signifies); but they <hi type="italic">brought thee forth;</hi> the pangs did not continue always; those that had <hi type="italic">travailed</hi> in convictions at last <hi type="italic">brought forth</hi> in consolations, and the <hi type="italic">pain was forgotten</hi> for joy of the Saviour's birth. By this very similitude our Saviour illustrates the joy which his disciples would have in his return to them, after a mournful separation for a time, <reference osisRef="John.16.21-John.16.22">John xvi. 21, 22</reference>. After the bitter pangs of repentance many a one has had the blessed birth of comfort; why then may not I? <div eID="gen15361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15362" type="x-p"/> 2. She begs of him that her union with him might be confirmed, and her communion with him continued and made more intimate (<reference osisRef="Song.8.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Set me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm.</hi> (1.) "Let me have a place in thy heart, an interest in thy love." This is that which all those desire above any thing that know how much their happiness is bound up in the love of Christ. (2.) "Let me never lose the room I have in thy heart; let thy love to me be ensured, as that deed which is sealed up not to be robbed. Let nothing ever prevail either to separate me from thy love, or, by suspending the communications of it, to deprive me of the comfortable sense of it." (3.) It comes in in a parenthesis, but in it gospel-grace lies as plain, and as much above ground, as any where in this mystical song: Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? Some make these the words of the bridegroom, expressing himself well pleased with her reliance on him and resignation of herself to his guidance. They are rather the words of the daughters of Jerusalem, to whom she spoke ( v. 4 ); they see her, and bless her. The angels in heaven, and all her friends on earth, are the joyful spectators of her bliss. The Jewish church came up from the wilderness supported by the divine power and favour, Deut. xxxii. 10, 11 . The Christian church was raised up from a low and desolate condition by the grace of Christ relied on, Gal. iv. 27 . Particular believers are amiable, nay, admirable, and divine grace is to be admired in them, when by the power of that grace they are brought up from the wilderness, leaning with a holy confidence and complacency upon Jesus Christ their beloved. This bespeaks the beauty of a soul, and the wonders of divine grace, 1. In the conversion of sinners. A sinful state is a wilderness, remote from communion with God, barren and dry, and in which there is no true comfort; it is a wandering wanting state. Out of this wilderness we are concerned to come up, by true repentance, in the strength of the grace of Christ, supported by our beloved and carried in his arms. 2. In the consolation of saints. A soul convinced of sin, and truly humbled for it, is in a wilderness, quite at a loss; and there is no coming out of this wilderness but leaning on Christ as our beloved, by faith, and not leaning to our own understanding, nor trusting to any righteousness or strength of our own as sufficient for us, but going forth, and going on, in the strength of the Lord God, and making mention of his righteousness, even his only, who is the Lord our righteousness. 3. ( Mark iv. 38 ), and the church ( Ps. xliv. 23 ), Awake, why sleepest thou? (3.) (2.) Love is a valiant victorious passion. The overflowing of these waters will strike no damp upon it, but it will enable a man to rejoice in tribulation. Though he slay me, I will love him and trust in him. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen15365" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Concern for the Gentiles; Privileges and Duties of the Church.</title> <div sID="gen15366" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts: what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for? <hi type="super">9</hi> If she <hi type="italic">be</hi> a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she <hi type="italic">be</hi> a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar. <hi type="super">10</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a wall, and my breasts like towers: then was I in his eyes as one that found favour. <hi type="super">11</hi> Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard unto keepers; every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand <hi type="italic">pieces</hi> of silver. <hi type="super">12</hi> My vineyard, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, <hi type="italic">is</hi> before me: thou, O Solomon, <hi type="italic">must have</hi> a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred. <div eID="gen15366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15367" type="x-p"/> Christ and his spouse having sufficiently confirmed their love to each other, and agreed it to be on both sides <hi type="italic">strong as death</hi> and inviolable, they are here, in these verses, like a loving husband and his wife, consulting together about their affairs, and considering what they should do. Yoke-fellows, having laid their hearts together, lay their heads together, to contrive about their relations and about their estates; and, accordingly, this happy pair are here advising with one another about a sister, and a vineyard. <div eID="gen15367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15368" type="x-p"/> I. They are here consulting about their sister, their little sister, and the disposing of her. <div eID="gen15368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15369" type="x-p"/> 1. The spouse proposes her case with a compassionate concern (<reference osisRef="Song.8.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have a little sister and she has no breasts</hi> (she has not grown up to maturity); <hi type="italic">what shall we do for</hi> this <hi type="italic">little sister</hi> of <hi type="italic">ours in the day that she shall be spoken for,</hi> so as that we may do well for her? (1.) This may be understood as spoken by the Jewish church concerning the Gentile world. God has espoused the church of the Jews to himself, and she was richly endowed, but what shall become of the poor Gentiles, <hi type="italic">the barren that has not borne,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the desolate?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>. Their condition (say the pious Jews) is very deplorable and forlorn; they are <hi type="italic">sisters,</hi> children of the same fathers, God and Adam, but they are <hi type="italic">little,</hi> because not dignified with the knowledge of God; they <hi type="italic">have no breasts,</hi> no divine revelation, no scriptures, no ministers, no breasts of consolation drawn out to them, when they might suck, being <hi type="italic">strangers to the covenants of promise,</hi> no breasts of instruction themselves to draw out to their children, to nourish them, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.2">1 Pet. ii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">What shall we do for</hi> them? We can but pity them, and pray for them. Lord, what wilt thou do for them? navigation_sections.content_plain: The affections between Christ and his spouse are as strong and lively here, in this closing chapter of the song, as ever, and rather more so. I. The spouse continues her importunity for a more intimate communion and fellowship with him, ver. 1-3 . II. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to interrupt her communion with her beloved ( ver. 4 ); and they, thereupon, admire her dependence on him, ver. 5 . III. She begs of her beloved, whom she raises up by her prayers ( ver. 5 ), that he would by his grace confirm that blessed union with him to which she was admitted, ver. 6, 7 . IV. She makes intercession for others also, that care might be taken of them ( ver. 8, 9 ), and pleases herself with the thoughts of her own interest in Christ and his affection to her, ver. 10 . V. She owns herself his tenant for a vineyard she held of him at Baal-hamon, ver. 11, 12 . VI. The song concludes with an interchanging of parting requests. Christ charges his spouse that she should often let him hear from her ( ver. 13 ), and she begs of him that he would hasten his return to her, ver. 14 ).
